planting.note: Sow directly into a constantly damp mineral crevice or tufa seep bed in fall for natural winter stratification; unlike dry scree saxifrages this one needs a spot that never fully dries out.

directions: Yellow mountain saxifrage creeps into loose trailing mats of narrow fleshy leaves and opens clusters of bright yellow to orange-speckled star flowers through early summer. It is a circumboreal plant of dripping calcareous rock and streamside ledges, documented along cold, wave-splashed basalt shoreline outcrops of Lake Superior including Isle Royale, where seepage keeps its roots constantly wet even as nearby rock bakes in the sun. Rock-garden growers keep it in a perpetually moist crevice, bog trough, or shaded tufa wall and give it an afternoon-shaded aspect at lower latitudes to avoid summer heat stress, since drying out even briefly will kill it. It increases slowly by creeping offsets that can be lifted and replanted to extend a planting.

planting.note: Set unrooted hardwood cuttings or rooted liners into loose sand in early spring while the ground is still cool and damp; this willow roots easily from cuttings and is the standard propagation method used in shoreline stabilization plantings.

directions: Sand-dune willow grows as a broad, suckering multi-stemmed shrub with downy gray-green leaves and stout catkins that emerge before leaf-out, forming thickets that knit together loose, shifting sand along Great Lakes beaches and foredunes. Its spreading root system is what makes it valuable for erosion control, and restoration nurseries propagate it specifically for dune and streambank stabilization work rather than ornamental borders. In a garden setting it suits a large, exposed sandy bank where its suckering habit has room to roam and its early catkins can feed emerging pollinators. It tolerates salt spray, burial by shifting sand, and periodic high water better than most woody plants.

planting.note: Sow into a lean, sharply drained scree or trough mix in fall; the seed needs a full season of cold before it will break dormancy, and seedlings resent any winter wet sitting around the crown.

directions: Boreal sandwort grows as a tiny, tufted cushion of needle-fine leaves studded in summer with small white five-petaled flowers held just above the foliage. It is a true arctic-alpine disjunct, persisting on exposed basalt and conglomerate rock barrens along the Lake Superior shoreline, including Isle Royale, far south of its main range across the Canadian Arctic. Alpine specialists grow it in a scree trough or raised crevice bed where drainage is sharp and the crown stays dry, since it is adapted to thin rocky ground rather than garden soil. It is traded almost entirely among rock-garden society seed exchanges and specialist alpine growers rather than general nurseries.

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing to speed germination, and set into lean gritty soil in spring; like most milkvetches it dislikes being transplanted once its taproot has formed.

directions: Alpine milkvetch is a low, sprawling legume with soft pinnate leaves and short spikes of pale lavender to whitish pea flowers, followed by small inflated pods. Its North American range is mostly subarctic and western alpine, but it turns up as a cold-relict disjunct on open gravel and rock barrens along the Lake Superior shoreline, a legacy of the glacial period when arctic tundra reached much farther south. Rock-garden growers raise it from seed in a lean scree bed or gravel trough that mimics the open mineral ground it needs, and it is passed around mainly through rock-garden society seed exchanges rather than retail nurseries. Established plants form a modest taproot and resent rich soil or heavy mulch, which encourages rot more than growth.

subcategory: Great Lakes cliff and shoreline rock-garden perennial

planting.note: Sow onto a vertical or sloped rock crevice bed in fall so the seed overwinters outdoors; this small mustard needs sharp drainage around its crown and will rot in flat, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Rock whitlow-grass makes a small tuft of narrow, slightly toothed leaves topped in spring by short racemes of tiny white four-petaled flowers, followed by flattened seedpods that persist into summer. It roots into limestone and dolomite cliff faces and cobble shoreline around the Great Lakes and locally in the Appalachians, favoring bare crevices where competition is minimal. Growers in the Draba-collecting corner of the rock-garden hobby keep it in a vertical tufa wall or crevice bed with sharp drainage, since it is adapted to cliff ledges rather than open ground. It is a seed-exchange and specialist-nursery plant rather than something found at a typical garden center.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat and sow in spring into lean, sharply drained gravelly soil; it forms a deep taproot early on and establishes poorly from transplanted divisions.

directions: Field locoweed forms a tight basal tuft of silvery, hairy pinnate leaves and sends up short stalks of pale yellow to cream pea-shaped flowers in a dense head. Mainly a plant of Arctic and high Rocky Mountain tundra, it survives as a glacial-relict disjunct on open gravel bars and rock outcrops along the Lake Superior shoreline well south of its main range. In cultivation it wants the same lean, mineral, fast-draining ground it uses in the wild, grown in a scree bed or trough rather than a border, and it is almost exclusively propagated from seed by rock-garden specialists and shared through society seed exchanges. Its silvery foliage stays attractive well after the short bloom period ends.
